simple: The source describes the actions. In a normal console program, your first action is inside main.
definition: In a hosted C environment, startup calls main. The form int main(void) returns an int and takes no arguments.
purpose: Build a minimal program to distinguish a toolchain problem from a problem in your source.
breakdown: #include makes the header declarations available.
Braces enclose the body of main.
return 0 reports successful termination.
observation: stdout contains Ready and a newline. Exit status 0 is separate from the printed text.
mistake: If puts has no declaration, check stdio.h. Fix a missing brace or semicolon in the source before running.

simple: Source files become object files. The linker connects references to definitions.
definition: Each source file goes through preprocessing. The Clang driver can compile with -c or carry the build through to an executable.
purpose: Use the failing stage to decide whether to inspect a source file or the build inputs.
form: clang -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.c worker.c -o report
example:
clang -std=c17 -c main.c -o main.o
clang -std=c17 -c worker.c -o worker.o
clang main.o worker.o -o report
breakdown: The commands are for native Clang.
The -c option stops before linking.
The last command links the two object files.
observation: If main.c sees a valid declaration of a function in worker.c, both compilations succeed. Removing worker.o can cause an unresolved definition at link time.
mistake: Including a declaration does not include its implementation. Add the source or object file to the build.

simple: Input data, the program result, and diagnostic messages use separate streams.
definition: stdio.h provides stdin, stdout, and stderr. puts writes a string and newline to stdout. fputs writes to the chosen stream without adding a newline.
purpose: Compare the exact task result independently of diagnostic messages and traces.
form:
puts(text);
fputs(text, stream);
example:
puts("accepted");
fputs("checked range\n", stderr);
breakdown: Read supplied input from stdin.
Use stdout for the result.
Keep diagnostics on stderr.
observation: stdout contains accepted plus a newline. stderr contains checked range plus the newline in its literal.
mistake: If an otherwise correct answer fails, look for debug text mixed into stdout. Move it to stderr or remove it.

simple: A format shows where values appear and how to print them.
definition: The printf family interprets a format string and its arguments. %d takes int, %ld takes long, %zu takes size_t, and %f in printf takes double.
purpose: Print the numbers, labels, and units required by the task contract.
form:
printf("label %d\n", value);
fprintf(stream, "%zu\n", count);
breakdown: Ordinary characters go directly to output.
Each conversion matches its argument's position and type.
%.2f shows two digits after the decimal point.
observation: In the C numeric locale the line is 3 items, 1.25 kg followed by a newline.
mistake: Using %d for size_t can cause undefined behavior. Match the format to the type instead of changing a type to silence a warning.

simple: A type determines what values can be stored and how operations treat them.
definition: int and long are signed integer types, double is a floating-point type, and char can store a character. Exact ranges depend on the implementation.
purpose: Choose a type from the meaning and range of your data. Give it an initial value when you know one.
breakdown: 12 has type int, and L gives 12500L type long.
1.5 is a double literal.
Single quotes enclose a character constant.
observation: boxes is 12, cents is 12500, rate is 1.5, and grade holds the value of B. Find implementation limits in limits.h and float.h.
mistake: A local int boxes; without initialization has no established value. Assign it before reading. The width of int depends on the implementation.

simple: Dividing two integers discards the fraction. Converting one operand first permits a fractional average.
definition: C17 integer division truncates toward zero. The remainder reconstructs the dividend as total == full * groups + left when the quotient is representable.
purpose: Find complete groups and leftovers or a fractional average. First check the divisor.
breakdown: 17 / 4 gives four complete groups.
17 % 4 leaves one item.
(double)total converts the operand before division.
observation: 4 * 4 + 1 reconstructs 17. The fractional result is 4.25.
mistake: (double)(total / groups) gives 4.0 after losing the fraction. Separately exclude a zero divisor and an unrepresentable integer quotient.

simple: Reading a numeric prefix is only the start. Check the remaining string and the allowed range.
definition: strtol from stdlib.h returns a long and reports where it stopped through its second argument. errno from errno.h helps detect values outside the range of long.
purpose: Parse the line before calculating. Decide whether the contract accepts whitespace, a sign, and a line ending.
breakdown: Clear errno so a previous error cannot be mistaken for this one.
end == text detects that no conversion took place.
This example requires the end of the string and a value in 0–999.
observation: 42 is accepted, 42x is rejected for its suffix, and 1000 is rejected by the task range. Explicitly allow trailing whitespace when required.
mistake: Both 0 and nonnumeric text can return 0. Inspect end and errno first.

simple: Check that an access is safe before touching the data.
definition: if selects a branch according to whether its condition is nonzero. && evaluates the right side only if the left is true, and || does so only if the left is false.
purpose: Guard array access, input ranges, and other prerequisites before computing.
breakdown: The first check excludes negatives.
The second compares the index with count before narrowing.
The array access runs only after both checks.
observation: With {8, 13} and count = 2, input 1 prints 13. Index 2 produces invalid.
mistake: <= count would allow one past the last item. In C, 0 <= index < count compares the intermediate 0 or 1 with count. Use two separate comparisons.

simple: Each pass handles one index while that index is below the array length.
definition: In a for loop, initialization runs once, the condition is checked before each pass, and the update follows the loop body.
purpose: Traverse a known number of items or repeat an operation a fixed number of times.
breakdown: i starts at 0.
The sizeof expression uses the actual array in scope.
After each pass, ++i prepares the next index.
observation: The example prints 3, 6, and 9 on separate lines. With an explicit count of 0 the body is skipped.
mistake: Check the final index and the empty range. Using i <= count takes an extra pass.

simple: Reading gets the next character or a signal that there is no character to process.
definition: while tests before its body. getchar returns the character as int or EOF. ferror(stdin) distinguishes an error from end-of-input.
purpose: Stop at the end of the first line or stream when the number of characters is unknown.
breakdown: Reading happens in the condition.
break stops the loop at LF.
int retains the result until the EOF check.
observation: Input AB followed by LF prints AB without a newline. With empty input the body is skipped.
mistake: If the final character repeats, check that each condition reads a new value. Do not narrow the result to char before comparing with EOF.

simple: Before calling, know what the function takes and what it promises to return.
definition: A prototype describes parameter types and the return type. A contract adds meaning, prerequisites, and guarantees a type alone cannot express.
purpose: Split the task into operations you can verify independently.
form: int larger(int left, int right);
breakdown: A prototype can go in a header.
The definition supplies the body that fulfills the promise.
The conditional operator chooses one value and still works when they are equal.
observation: larger(3, 8) gives 8, larger(-2, -7) gives -2, and larger(5, 5) gives 5.
mistake: Two int parameters are not generally interchangeable. Describe the meaning and order of the arguments.

simple: A function gets the argument's value in its own parameter.
definition: C initializes parameters with argument values. Changing a parameter does not itself change the caller's object. A pointer also passes by value.
purpose: Check the caller's variable separately from the return value.
form: int step(int current);
breakdown: current receives a copy of previous.
++current changes the local current.
return passes the new value to next.
observation: If previous is 5, next becomes 6 and previous stays 5.
mistake: step(previous); discards the returned value. To change previous, assign the result or define a separate pointer contract.

simple: Scope tells you where a name is visible. Lifetime tells you whether the object still exists.
definition: An ordinary automatic local object's lifetime is limited to execution of its block. Objects with static storage duration follow different rules.
purpose: Copy a value into an outer object before the inner work ends.
breakdown: saved is declared outside.
measured is created inside and copied as a number.
After the block the program prints saved's own value.
observation: The result is 12. The name measured cannot be used after its block.
mistake: Saving &measured would preserve an address without extending the object's lifetime. Do not read through it after the block.

simple: Calculate the expected value first. Then compare it with the function call.
definition: assert from assert.h checks that the expression is nonzero. Defining NDEBUG when including the header disables the check.
purpose: Check ordinary data, ties, and boundaries before combining program parts.
form: assert(actual == expected);
breakdown: The expected value is written to the right of ==.
Both inputs to the first case are negative.
The tie checks that equality yields a valid response.
observation: A correct larger passes both checks silently. Change an expected value to see a failure in a testing build.
mistake: Do not put operations required by the program inside assert. With NDEBUG the expression is not evaluated.

simple: Indexing starts at zero. With length 3, the final index is 2.
definition: An array is a sequence of elements of the same type. sizeof an array object gives its byte size. Dividing by an element size gives the length.
purpose: Find the count and traverse only items that actually exist.
form:
int sample[] = {5, 8, 13};
size_t count = sizeof sample / sizeof sample[0];
breakdown: The initializer determines the length of sample.
Dividing the sizes while sample is an array gives count = 3.
count - 1 is the final index only when count > 0.
observation: last is 13. For a possibly empty range, check its count before evaluating count - 1.
mistake: sample[count] is out of bounds. In a function parameter, sizeof that name does not give the array length.

simple: Pass the address of the first element and the number of elements the function may use.
definition: A const int values[] parameter is adjusted to const int *. This pointer carries no count. The caller supplies it separately.
purpose: Use one function to read arrays of different lengths under explicit bounds.
form: long sum(const int values[], size_t count);
breakdown: count defines the valid range [0, count).
const prevents writes through values.
The sum must fit in long for this function.
observation: For {2, 4, 8}, count 2 gives 6 and count 3 gives 14.
mistake: Do not compute sizeof values / sizeof values[0] inside sum. sizeof values gives the pointer size.

simple: On each pass, update the running result with the next item.
definition: An invariant describes what the running result means after processing the prefix seen so far. A maximum over an empty range needs a separate rule.
purpose: Verify a statistic by explaining the state after every pass.
breakdown: The sum form starts with 0 for an empty prefix.
The nonempty example starts the maximum with an actual item.
The loop replaces it only when it finds a greater value.
observation: For {-5, -2, -9}, maximum changes from -5 to -2 and stays -2.
mistake: Starting maximum at 0 gives 0 for an all-negative array. Check that the range is nonempty and initialize from the first item.

simple: Sorting uses a function that says how two items are ordered.
definition: qsort from stdlib.h reorders the elements of the supplied array. Its comparator receives element addresses and returns a negative value, zero, or a positive value for their order.
purpose: Separate comparison from sorting. Test duplicate and extreme values.
form: qsort(values, count, sizeof values[0], compare_int);
breakdown: void * gives an item address without a declared item type.
Casting and dereferencing read the corresponding int object.
Subtracting comparison results is safe because each result is 0 or 1.
observation: Sorting {6, -1, 6, 2} ascending gives {-1, 2, 6, 6}. The relative order of equal items is not guaranteed.
mistake: Avoid return a - b for arbitrary int inputs because the signed difference can overflow.

simple: A string ends at a zero byte. That byte takes space but does not count as text length.
definition: A C string is a sequence of characters terminated by its first null character. strlen counts the bytes before it.
purpose: Reserve room for text and the terminator. Check the bound before calling library routines.
form:
char name[] = "Go";
size_t length = strlen(name);
example:
char name[] = {'G', 'o', '\0'};
printf("%zu / %zu\n", strlen(name), sizeof name);
breakdown: The array stores G, o, and a zero.
strlen finds two bytes before the zero.
sizeof counts all three elements of the array.
observation: The output is 2 / 3. The empty string has length zero and its literal still takes one byte.
mistake: {'G', 'o'} without a zero is not a string for strlen. Add a terminator or use an explicit length for byte operations.

simple: Reading leaves room in the buffer and preserves the line feed if it fits.
definition: For a limit greater than 1, fgets reads up to limit - 1 characters, through a line feed, or to end-of-input, and terminates a successful result with a zero.
purpose: Read into a bounded buffer, then check separately that it represents a complete line under the task rules.
breakdown: Size 8 leaves room for seven characters and the terminator.
strchr from string.h looks for LF in the successfully read string.
Replacing LF with zero removes that line ending.
observation: With ABC followed by LF, stdout contains [ABC]. For input longer than seven bytes this snippet only prints the prefix.
mistake: No LF can mean a short final line or a full buffer with unread input. Check further when the contract requires a complete line.

simple: Compare string contents rather than pointer values.
definition: strcmp from string.h compares strings up to a difference or the terminator and reports the sign of the result. Zero means equality.
purpose: Recognize a complete command and distinguish it from a similar prefix.
form: int matches = strcmp(actual, expected) == 0;
breakdown: Both arguments must be valid strings.
== 0 checks complete equality.
A positive or negative result describes order without promising a particular number.
observation: With report, stdout contains matched. A string with an added space or word does not match.
mistake: command == "report" compares pointers. Use strcmp after confirming both strings are terminated.

simple: A pointer holds an address. Dereferencing uses the object at that address.
definition: & obtains an object's address. * declares a pointer type or, in an expression, accesses the object when the pointer permits it.
purpose: Give a function access to an existing object and verify that the original object changed.
form:
int *pointer = &object;
int copy = *pointer;
breakdown: &temperature produces a pointer to temperature.
int *p declares a pointer to int.
*p = 20 stores a value in temperature.
observation: After the assignment, temperature is 20. Changing a copy made with int copy = *p would leave temperature unchanged.
mistake: Do not dereference an uninitialized, null, or invalid pointer. Establish which object it refers to first.

simple: Adding 1 to a pointer advances it by one element.
definition: Pointer arithmetic stays within one array or reaches the position immediately past its end. You may compare a one-past pointer during traversal but may not dereference it.
purpose: Traverse a range when a function already has an address and count.
breakdown: values becomes the first element's address in this expression.
values + 3 is the end position for three int elements.
The condition stops before reading that position.
observation: The example prints 2, 5, and 8 with spaces and a trailing space. An empty range with a valid starting pointer skips the body.
mistake: Advancing beyond past does not produce a valid pointer. Check the index and count before computing an address.

simple: A function can return a status and store data in a caller-owned object.
definition: The pointer value is passed by copy. Dereferencing accesses the original object. The contract determines when writing is allowed.
purpose: Distinguish a failed call from a valid result such as zero.
form: int operation(int input, int *out);
breakdown: The caller passes &result.
For NULL the function returns 0 before storing.
On success it stores in *out and returns 1.
observation: Pass -7 and &result: status is 1 and result becomes 0. For NULL the status is 0.
mistake: A NULL check does not check object lifetime. Pass a live, writable int and read the result only after success.

simple: const restricts writes through a pointer. NULL denotes no pointed-to object.
definition: const int * treats the object as const int through that pointer. The pointer itself can be reassigned. A null pointer can be compared but not dereferenced.
purpose: Describe read-only access and handle an absent object according to the contract.
form:
const int *read_only = &value;
if (read_only != NULL) { /* read */ }
breakdown: &value points to a live int.
const int * allows reading that int through read_only.
Dereferencing and copying saves the number, not its address.
observation: copy is 7. After value = 9, copy stays 7 while another read through read_only yields 9.
mistake: Do not cast away const to write. If the object was defined as const, the write has undefined behavior.

simple: A structure groups related values into one record.
definition: struct declares named members. Use . on the object and -> on a pointer to the object.
purpose: Keep ID and value together so you can pass or validate a record as a unit.
form: struct Reading { int id; int value; };
breakdown: Designated initializers match values to fields.
row->value is equivalent to (*row).value.
An array of structures stores a sequence of these records.
observation: After the assignment, reading.value is 18 and reading.id remains 7.
mistake: Do not use == to compare structures. Compare the relevant fields. Structure assignment does copy the structure value.

simple: Give states names so the meaning of a condition is visible.
definition: enum declares a type and named integer constants. By default the first constant is zero and each following one is the preceding value plus one.
purpose: Separate a missing record, invalid data, and success without unexplained numbers.
form: enum Status { STATUS_OK, STATUS_MISSING, STATUS_INVALID };
breakdown: The enumerators name three distinct outcomes.
status holds the selected state.
The condition compares a meaningful name instead of a number.
observation: The example prints missing. With STATUS_OK it skips that branch.
mistake: Do not assume an arbitrary number is valid just because you assigned it to an enum. Validate input and confirm it maps to an allowed state.

simple: Ensure the number of elements times the element size is representable before multiplying.
definition: malloc takes a byte count of type size_t. Unsigned multiplication can wrap to a smaller size. SIZE_MAX is declared in stdint.h.
purpose: Allocate enough storage for the accepted number of elements.
form: if (count > SIZE_MAX / sizeof *items) { /* reject */ }
breakdown: Compare count with the maximum quotient before multiplying.
sizeof *items follows the element type.
This contract rejects zero capacity separately. Check malloc for NULL afterward.
observation: With count = 3 and sizeof(int) = 4, the request is 12 bytes. A count above the safe limit is rejected before multiplying.
mistake: Checking only malloc's result cannot catch the wrapped product. Allocation of the smaller size may succeed.

simple: An acquired block needs somebody responsible for releasing it on every exit path.
definition: malloc from stdlib.h returns allocated storage or NULL on a failed nonzero request. malloc does not initialize the storage. free ends its lifetime.
purpose: Keep responsibility for a block explicit when a function receives or returns a pointer.
form:
int *items = malloc(count * sizeof *items);
if (items == NULL) { /* handle failure */ }
breakdown: Check allocation before writing.
Store 21 before reading uninitialized storage.
The owner calls free once and then clears its pointer variable.
observation: Successful allocation prints 21. Allocation failure exits before dereferencing.
mistake: Setting the owner's pointer to NULL after free leaves the old values in other copies. Stop using all such copies.

simple: Request the new size through a temporary pointer. Keep the owner until success is known.
definition: With a nonzero new size, realloc may move the block. Failure preserves the old allocation. On success, use the returned pointer.
purpose: Grow a dynamic array while preserving items and a consistent capacity.
breakdown: Check the size and require nonzero capacity first.
Store the result in grown.
On success, update items and capacity together.
observation: When growing, the old initial elements are preserved. On failure, the original pointer and capacity remain usable.
mistake: items = realloc(items, n) can lose the only address on failure. After success, obtain element addresses again from the new pointer.

simple: First acquire a stream. When finished, check the close result.
definition: fopen from stdio.h returns FILE * or NULL. rb reads an existing binary stream, wb creates or truncates a file, and ab appends to it.
purpose: Distinguish path failure, an empty file, and failed output. Choose the mode before opening.
form:
FILE *stream = fopen(path, "rb");
if (stream == NULL) { /* handle failure */ }
breakdown: The file name must match the path in the working area.
NULL means open failed.
fclose returns 0 on success or EOF on failure.
observation: An existing empty input/reading.txt can open and close with status 0. A missing file gives status 1 before fclose.
mistake: fclose(NULL) is invalid. Opening with wb truncates an existing file even if the program stops before writing.

simple: Copy the bytes actually read and check for failure independently of end-of-file.
definition: fgetc returns a byte as int or EOF. fread and fwrite return the number of items processed. With item size 1 that count is in bytes.
purpose: Make an exact copy with line endings preserved and short writes handled.
form:
size_t n = fread(buffer, 1, capacity, input);
size_t written = fwrite(buffer, 1, n, output);
breakdown: The condition reads the next byte.
Check fputc for EOF after every write.
ferror(input) distinguishes read failure from normal end-of-file.
observation: On binary streams, 3, LF, 6, LF copies as four bytes. Empty input writes zero bytes.
mistake: while (!feof(input)) checks before attempting a read and can use an invalid final result. Check the read result instead.

simple: Find field boundaries and validate the whole row before adding a record.
definition: In TSV, a tab separates fields. The contract defines the field count, ranges, line endings, and permitted duplicates.
purpose: Parse a writable copy whose length is already checked. Validate separators independently of field contents.
form:
char *separator = strchr(row, '\t');
if (separator == NULL) { /* reject the row */ }
breakdown: strchr finds the first tab in a terminated string.
The second call rejects an extra separator.
Replacing the tab with zero creates two strings for number validation.
observation: 7 TAB 15 separates into 7 and 15. 7 TAB 15 TAB 2 is rejected before checking numbers.
mistake: Splitting fields does not validate ranges, uniqueness, or suffixes. Perform those checks before increasing the record count.

simple: Release acquired resources on every path and preserve the first failure reason.
definition: A state variable records whether a resource was acquired. Cleanup logic separates releasing the resource from selecting an error message.
purpose: Check that a write failure still closes the file and remains visible if a later action fails.
breakdown: output != NULL guards the close.
fclose is on the left of &&, so an existing problem does not prevent it.
The right side permits recording the close error only when no earlier error exists.
observation: The example keeps write-error even when closing fails. If problem is initially NULL, a close failure becomes the first error.
mistake: problem == NULL && fclose(output) == EOF would skip fclose after an earlier failure. Separate resource release from recording the message.

simple: A successful calculation and its output file are separate things to verify.
definition: A C program writes bytes in the run's file area. The Nexus delta lists new or changed files. Saving a result into the project is separate.
purpose: Check the report path and exact contents before downloading or saving.
breakdown: wb opens the file to replace its contents.
The write and close are checked separately.
The file is opened in that run's file area.
observation: totals.tsv contains records TAB total LF and 2 TAB 3 LF. If the file already had those exact bytes, the Nexus delta is empty.
mistake: Exit status 0 alone does not show the report contents. Open the file and compare bytes. If you need it in the editor, save it explicitly.

simple: Directives choose and replace program text before execution.
definition: The preprocessor works with tokens. #if selects a branch before compilation. A function-like macro substitutes its argument tokens into a replacement.
purpose: Build variants with an explicit mode and predictable argument grouping.
form:
#define CAPACITY 8
#define TOTAL(count) ((count) * CAPACITY)
example:
#define MODE 2
#if MODE == 2
#define CAPACITY 12
#else
#define CAPACITY 8
#endif
#define TOTAL(count) ((count) * CAPACITY)
/* Inside a function: int items = TOTAL(1 + 2); */
breakdown: MODE selects CAPACITY 12.
TOTAL(1 + 2) becomes ((1 + 2) * 12).
Rebuild for header changes to take effect.
observation: items is 36. With MODE 1 and a rebuild it is 24.
mistake: Without grouping, 1 + 2 * CAPACITY has a different result. If a macro uses an argument more than once, avoid arguments with side effects.

simple: Two paths to the same header should yield one structure definition in a source file.
definition: Conditional preprocessing under a unique macro skips the header body when it is included again in the same translation unit.
purpose: Keep needed dependencies without duplicate definitions.
form:
#ifndef MODULE_H
#define MODULE_H
/* public declarations */
#endif
example:
#ifndef GAUGE_H
#define GAUGE_H
struct Gauge { int millimetres; };
#endif
breakdown: The first #ifndef enters because GAUGE_H is not yet defined.
#define marks the header as seen.
Another include path to the same file skips the body.
observation: Including gauge.h twice yields one struct Gauge definition in the preprocessed source.
mistake: Mismatched names in #ifndef and #define break the guard. Different headers also need different guard names.

simple: A header describes the available calls. Helpers can stay inside the source file.
definition: Declarations tell callers the types. A file-scope static function has internal linkage. The definition of a public function links to call sites.
purpose: Offer a stable call while keeping the choice of internal rules in the implementation.
form:
/* gauge.h */
int remaining_litres(int used);
breakdown: gauge.h declares remaining_litres.
gauge.c includes its header to keep types consistent.
limit is local to this translation unit.
observation: remaining_litres(7) gives 5. Changing the internal limit to 10 gives 3 after a rebuild.
mistake: Putting an internal helper in the public header breaks the module boundary. Add the .c file to the build instead of using #include.

simple: Compare intermediate values and locate the first step at which the run disagrees with your expectation.
definition: A trace records observable results from individual steps. Debug messages on stderr preserve the exact stdout contract.
purpose: Locate a faulty condition without rewriting parsing and output together.
form: fprintf(stderr, "name=%d\n", value);
breakdown: The two flags are computed independently.
stderr shows both values.
stdout reports only the final decision.
observation: For value = 70 the trace reads below=0 above=0, and the answer is accepted. For 71 it reads below=0 above=1, and the answer is invalid.
mistake: Checking only the final invalid line can hide whether parsing or range checking failed. Keep the input fixed and compare the trace.

simple: A warning appears during a build. A sanitizer can detect a failure during a particular run.
definition: Compiler options enable different checks. -fsyntax-only checks source without creating an executable. A sanitizer adds monitoring to executable code.
purpose: Use native diagnostics alongside contract checks with small reproducible cases.
form: clang -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -fsyntax-only main.c
example:
clang -std=c17 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined main.c -o check
./check
breakdown: The first command checks source with warnings.
The second build enables AddressSanitizer and checks for selected undefined behavior.
Only a run with test inputs exercises the added checks.
observation: An ordinary case can compile and pass while a boundary fails. A sanitizer reports a specific problem it detected on the path taken.
mistake: Clean sanitizer output does not cover unseen paths. These commands need native Clang and its runtime libraries; an ordinary WASI run is separate.

simple: Test the boundary and the nearest value outside. Keep the input that revealed the problem.
definition: A regression check repeats the exact original input and observations after a change. A boundary case distinguishes adjacent branches.
purpose: Record expected stdout, stderr and exit status for exact input bytes, so a fix can be checked again.
breakdown: 9 and 10 test the lower boundary.
18 and 19 test the upper boundary.
For parsing, add 12x separately from valid 12.
observation: The in_range results are 0, 1, 1, 0 in order. The project parser must also reject the unwanted suffix.
mistake: Replacing the failing input after the fix loses the evidence. Repeat the same bytes and check a neighbouring accepted case separately.

simple: Validate the starting records first. Commands change only what the contract allows.
definition: This project loads unique IDs within capacity, reads or updates an existing item, and writes the report in the agreed order.
purpose: Verify one chain from the input file through the in-memory change to an exact report.
form:
const Record *inventory_find(const Inventory *stock, int id);
int inventory_set(Inventory *stock, int id, int quantity);
breakdown: find returns a pointer for reading or NULL.
set updates an existing quantity and reports success.
A second find reveals the change separately from an ok message.
observation: If ID 20 existed with quantity 0 and set succeeds, the second read prints 20 7. The source file would change only through a separate write, which is absent here.
mistake: Do not report after a failed load or use set to insert an unknown ID. Check the operation's outcome before continuing.
